How the scenario responses scale with the substitution share ρ

The reported responses are proportional to ρ to within a few per cent, and the sign-pattern regimes do not depend on it. The contained-contraction regime does: it is a threshold label, and as ρ rises most contained partner responses cross the threshold at a ρ this report gives run by run.

Every number below is computed in this document from those three files.

Status of claims: measured. The cause of the ρ = 1 failures is inferred, not traced, and is marked as such.

What was run

Every intervention moves a share ρ of the primary sector’s demand to its substitute (Scenario design, §4.1); the paper reports ρ = 0.2. The question is whether the reported responses — and the cross-border regimes built on them — depend on that choice. The 24 gold-closure high-finance credit runs (twelve interventions × the EU/RoW and North/South setups) were re-made at ρ = 0.1, 0.4 and 0.7, and at ρ = 1.0 for the eight production interventions and 0.9 for the four final-demand ones.

Why 0.9 for the final-demand interventions. At ρ = 1.0 all eight final-demand runs (sc1–sc4, both setups) stop at t = 70, the shock period, on the first iteration, with an NA in the credit-rationing step (model/code/MVP_model_2026.R:1026). At ρ = 1 the primary sector’s whole share in that channel moves, so a share reaches exactly zero; a 0/0 there is the likely cause (inferred, not traced). ρ = 1 is a corner of the operator, not a policy anyone proposes, so the engine was not changed. All eight run at ρ = 0.9.

The response is the one the paper reports: the mean over t = 79…100 of the percentage deviation from the run’s own baseline (the current account as a level difference, since it crosses zero).

Responses are proportional to ρ

Each run and variable is fitted through the origin (ρ = 0 is the baseline) in two ways: the line y = bρ, whose uncentred R² is 1 when the response is exactly proportional, and the quadratic y = β₁ρ + β₂ρ², whose ratio β₂/β₁ is the relative departure from proportionality at ρ = 1.

The median R² is above 0.999 for every variable and region. The largest curvature ratios (8 fits with |β₂/β₁| > 1, up to 5.7) belong to runs whose response is close to zero: the median |response at ρ = 0.2| of those fits is 0.0006, so β₁ is small and the ratio is not a measure of nonlinearity.

The regimes

The cross-border regime of a run is read from the signs of the two regions’ value-added responses: production leakage (PL: the intervening region contracts, the partner expands), competitive displacement (CD: the reverse), dual contraction (DC), dual expansion (DE), and contained contraction (CC: the partner’s |response| is below τ = 0.003%).

Sign-pattern regimes do not depend on ρ. All 14 runs with a sign-pattern regime (PL, CD, DC or DE) at ρ = 0.2 keep it at every ρ tested, except that a run’s partner response can drop below τ at ρ = 0.1, where everything is half as large (0 runs do not meet this test). Proportionality is what makes this so: if both responses scale with ρ, their signs cannot change.

Contained contraction does depend on ρ. Of the 10 runs contained at ρ = 0.2, 7 cross τ inside the grid, at ρ between 0.22 and 0.89, and become a sign-pattern regime; 3 stay below τ at every ρ. CC is a threshold on a partner response that grows linearly with ρ, so it holds at the reported share and, for most such runs, only below some share.

What follows for the paper

  • The responses can be read as ρ times a per-unit effect; the ranking of interventions does not depend on the choice ρ = 0.2.
  • The four sign-pattern regimes are robust to ρ. The contained-contraction regime should be stated as conditional on the substitution share, with the crossing values above.
  • ρ = 1 is not needed and is not run for the final-demand interventions; 0.9 stands in for the top of the range.
